Tax preparers are financial institutions, as far as the FTC is concerned

What the FTC Safeguards Rule asks of a small tax or accounting office, and what to get done before tax season.

Published
November 12, 2026
Topic
Local questions
For
Owners of small tax, bookkeeping, and accounting offices
On this page 8 sections
  1. Why the rule reaches tax offices
  2. What the rule asks for
  3. The 30-day clock
  4. The IRS asks too
  5. One thing to tell your clients this week
  6. What to get done before January
  7. Going further
  8. Sources

A couple has had their taxes done at the same small office for years. In February they come in, sign, and e-file, the way they always do. A day later the return bounces: one was already filed under their Social Security number. Somebody got there first, with their names, their income, and a refund sent to an account they've never seen. In its 2025 report to Congress, the National Taxpayer Advocate described identity theft victims waiting an average of more than 21 months for the IRS to sort cases like this out. That's nearly two years of a family waiting on money they were counting on.

The thief didn't need to break into the IRS. Everything it took to file that return sits in a tax preparer's client folder: Social Security numbers for the whole household, income, prior returns, and the bank account for the refund. People hand all of that over once a year without thinking twice, because they trust the person across the desk. That trust is the business, and it's exactly what criminals go after.

The timing matters right now. The IRS just reminded taxpayers that its online tool for getting an Identity Protection PIN, the six-digit number that blocks anyone else from filing under a person's Social Security number, goes offline for annual maintenance on Monday, November 16, and doesn't come back until mid-January. The 2027 filing season opens soon after. So the next ten weeks are the window to get an office's own defenses in order before the busiest, most targeted stretch of the year.

Those defenses aren't optional, either. The Federal Trade Commission names tax preparation services as a "financial institution" under its Safeguards Rule, whether you work alone at a kitchen table or run a ten-person firm. Here's what the rule asks, in plain words, and what you can get done before January.

Why the rule reaches tax offices

The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act requires financial institutions to protect their customers' personal information. Banks answer to their own regulators. For most other businesses that offer financial services to consumers, tax preparers included, the FTC enforces it through the Safeguards Rule, 16 CFR Part 314.

The FTC rewrote the rule in 2021 to spell out specific requirements, and most of them took effect on June 9, 2023. A later amendment added a duty to report certain breaches to the FTC, starting May 13, 2024. If the rule feels new to you, that's because, in its current form, it mostly is.

What the rule asks for

The rule asks for a written information security program that fits your size and the sensitivity of what you hold. In the tax world it's usually called a WISP, a written information security plan. For a small office, it comes down to these pieces:

  • One person in charge. The rule calls this person the Qualified Individual. It can be you, someone on staff, or an outside provider. If it's a provider, you still own the result, and you name someone senior to oversee them.
  • Multi-factor authentication for anyone who signs in to a system holding client information: email, tax software, the client portal, cloud storage, and remote access. All of them, since a thief only needs the one you skipped.
  • Encryption of client information when it travels outside your network and when it's stored, including on laptops and backup drives.
  • Access limited to what each job needs, and a list of the systems, devices, and people that touch client data.
  • Security training for everyone, kept current as new tricks show up.
  • Contracts that require your service providers to protect the data, and a periodic check that they do. Your IT person, your software vendors, and any outside bookkeeper all count.
  • Secure disposal of a former client's information no later than two years after you last used it, unless you have a legal or business reason to keep it.
  • A written plan for what happens when something goes wrong: who decides, who gets told, and in what order.

If you keep information on fewer than 5,000 consumers, you can skip four of the formal pieces: the written risk assessment, penetration testing and scans, the written incident response plan, and the annual report to leadership. Everything else still applies, including MFA, encryption, and training. Count carefully before you lean on this. Former clients count, and an office that has been open a while usually holds more people's information than its current client list suggests.

The 30-day clock

Since May 13, 2024, if unencrypted information on 500 or more people is taken, you have to tell the FTC through a form on its website as soon as possible, and no later than 30 days after you find out. Encrypted data counts as unencrypted if the key was taken too. The FTC can publish these reports. New York's own breach notification law applies on top of that, with notices to the people affected and to the state.

This is where encryption earns its keep. A stolen laptop with an encrypted disk is a bad day and a police report. The same laptop without encryption can mean a federal filing, letters to every client on it, and a lot of explaining to people who trusted you.

The IRS asks too

The IRS comes at the same requirement from its side. Each time you apply for or renew your PTIN, Form W-12 asks you to confirm that you know paid preparers are required by law to create and maintain a written information security plan. The form points to two free IRS publications:

  • Publication 5708 is a sample WISP written for small tax and accounting practices. It's the best place to start.
  • Publication 4557 is the IRS guide to safeguarding taxpayer data, with checklists for the office.

One thing to tell your clients this week

Clients who want an IP PIN for the coming season should request one through their IRS online account before Monday, when the tool goes offline. Clients who already have one don't need to do anything: the IRS generates a new number for them each year, and they can see it in their account again from mid-January. A short note from you this week could spare one of them the wait described above. Remind them, too, that the IRS never calls, emails, or texts to ask for an IP PIN, and that they should share it only with you, when you're ready to file.

Keep the finished plan somewhere you can find it, and look at it again when something changes: a new hire, new software, or a second location. A plan that lives in a drawer protects no one.

Going further

For a longer walkthrough of the rule, with a staff checklist, a paperwork list, and a 20-day plan, see You Have 20 Seconds To Comply. For the training piece, Phish Out of Water is a one-hour session kit anyone can teach from. Both are free and open on GitHub, and you're welcome to use them without ever talking to me.

If you'd rather have help, this is work I do for small offices around Queens: setting up MFA, checking encryption and backups, drafting the plan from Publication 5708, and running the staff session. The first 15-minute call is free.

This post explains the rule in general terms. It isn't legal advice, and an attorney can tell you how it applies to your practice.

  • FTC Safeguards Rule: What Your Business Needs to Know, Federal Trade Commission: the FTC's plain-language guide to the rule.
  • Standards for Safeguarding Customer Information, notification amendment, Federal Register: the 30-day FTC notice, effective May 13, 2024.
  • IRS reminder: Take steps now to protect tax information, IRS (IR-2026-127, October 22, 2026): the IP PIN and the online tool's mid-November to mid-January maintenance window.
  • Get an Identity Protection PIN, IRS: who can get one, the yearly new number, and the system being offline from November 16, 2026, until mid-January 2027.
  • National Taxpayer Advocate delivers annual report to Congress, IRS (IR-2026-15): identity theft victims waiting an average of more than 21 months.
  • Form W-12, PTIN Application and Renewal, IRS: the line where preparers confirm they know a written information security plan is required.
